item.semiconductor-lab.lead_screw.note: Moves the coil slowly along the bar. Too fast and impurities cannot keep up.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_screw.note1: A long threaded rod: turn it and things move in a straight line.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_screw.note3: The distance moved per turn is the lead (pitch). Speed = lead × revolutions. A 1 mm lead screw turned once a minute moves 6 cm an hour, turning a motor's spin into a slow, precise straight-line motion.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_screw.note4: Around 1800 Henry Maudslay in England built an all-metal lathe whose tool carriage was driven by a lead screw, so accurate screws could be made identical again and again. The stages of today's chip lithography machines (ball screws) are its descendants.
block.semiconductor-lab.lathe.note1: A machine that spins material and cuts it with a tool to make round parts.
block.semiconductor-lab.lathe.note2: 750 W electric. Steel ingot -> pump rotor (30 s). Put a lead screw in the lower-left 'master screw' slot and steel -> 4 standard screws [8-02] (the lead screw is not used up). Parts made carry this lathe's size error. Recipe: 2 steel + lead screw + 2 iron + motor.
block.semiconductor-lab.lathe.note3: Around 1797-1800 Henry Maudslay in England built an all-metal lathe whose tool carriage was moved by a lead screw. The shaking of the hand was gone, and identical screws and parts could be made in any number. He is called the father of machine tools.
block.semiconductor-lab.lathe.note4: A lathe can remake its own lead screw more accurately (better screw -> better parts -> better screw). This cycle of machines making more accurate machines runs from precision engineering all the way to the nanometre stages of lithography machines.
block.semiconductor-lab.lathe.placeholde: Approximation: Maudslay's lathe was driven by hand, water wheel or steam; here by an electric motor. For now it only turns rotary pump rotors.
item.semiconductor-lab.pump_rotor.note1: A turned steel cylinder that spins inside a rotary pump.
item.semiconductor-lab.pump_rotor.note2: Turned from a steel ingot on the lathe. A part of the rotary pump [5-04]. It spins off-centre (eccentric), so the gap chamber grows and shrinks and pushes gas out.
item.semiconductor-lab.pump_rotor.note3: In 1905 Gaede built a 'rotary mercury pump' that moved air with a rotating part, turning the vacuum pump from a hand tool into a machine.
item.semiconductor-lab.pump_rotor.note4: The gap between rotor and casing is a few tens of micrometres. A larger gap lets gas leak back and spoils the vacuum, so the lathe's accuracy sets the pump's performance.
item.semiconductor-lab.simple_microscope: A tool with one small round lens that makes tiny, invisible things look big.

Crown lens + 2 copper. Hold a mask, original or wafer in your other hand and right-click to see whether one cell of its pattern is visible. With NA 0.2 it resolves about 1.4 um (masks up to contact and 1:1 projection printing).
In the 1670s the Dutch draper Leeuwenhoek used microscopes with a single tiny bead-like lens he ground himself (about 270x) and was the first to see microorganisms and bacteria in water.

The smaller and more strongly curved the lens, the higher the magnification, but it must be held right up to the eye. Leeuwenhoek kept his lens-making secret, and nobody else matched his lenses for a long time.
Approximation: NA 0.2 is a game value (⚠️ Leeuwenhoek's best lenses are said to have resolved about 1 um). The real mount was brass.
item.semiconductor-lab.compound_microsco: A microscope that magnifies in two stages, objective and eyepiece. Used to inspect fine lines on wafers and masks.

Achromatic lens (objective) + crown lens (eyepiece) + 2 copper + lead screw (focus) + iron. With NA 0.9 it resolves about 0.31 um (masks up to i-line steppers; lines finer than KrF cannot be seen with light).

In 1873 Abbe, working at the Zeiss works, showed that the finest line a microscope can resolve is about half the wavelength of light (d = lambda / 2NA), and that nothing finer can be seen with any lens. In 1878 he made oil-immersion lenses that raise the NA.

NA (numerical aperture) is how wide an angle of light the lens accepts. In air it cannot exceed 1, so to see finer you must shorten the wavelength (the UV microscope, 1904), fill the gap with oil or water (the same idea as immersion lithography [7-16]), or use electrons instead of light. Once chip lines became finer than the wavelength of light, inspection moved to electron microscopes.
Approximation: calculated with 550 nm, the middle of white light. Illumination techniques (Köhler) and oil immersion are omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.standard_screw.no: A screw cut to exactly the same shape as all the others. It fits any machine's nut.
Turn steel on a lathe with a lead screw in its 'master screw' slot: 4 screws (the lead screw is not used up). It carries the lathe's size error (measure it with calipers or a micrometer [8-04]).

Once every workshop had its own thread shapes, and each screw and nut were made as a matched pair. In 1841 Whitworth proposed a 55-degree thread angle and a set number of threads per size, and screws across Britain became uniform.

Maudslay's lathe moved its tool carriage with a master lead screw, so it could cut any number of screws with exactly the same pitch. If part shapes are fixed, any part fits (interchangeable parts) - the foundation of later mass production and car assembly lines.
item.semiconductor-lab.standard_screw.pl: Approximation: the error range (+-25 um) is a game value. Thread forms (55 degrees etc.) are not distinguished.
item.semiconductor-lab.vernier_caliper.n: A tool that grips things between two jaws to measure length or thickness. A small scale lets you read fine fractions.
2 bronze. Hold a lathe part in your other hand and right-click: reads to 0.05 mm. It cannot grade parts (0.01 mm differences); that needs a micrometer.

In 1631 the Frenchman Pierre Vernier devised a sliding scale slightly offset from the main scale (the vernier) to read fractions between marks. Calipers of today's shape were sold by Brown & Sharpe in the USA around 1851.

If 20 vernier divisions span 19 mm of the main scale, each differs by 0.05 mm. Find where a vernier line exactly meets a main-scale line and you read that fraction (the eye is very sensitive to misaligned lines).
item.semiconductor-lab.vernier_caliper.p: Approximation: real calipers were brass (copper + zinc); here they are made of bronze.
item.semiconductor-lab.micrometer.note1: A tool that grips things by turning a screw and measures to 0.01 mm.
item.semiconductor-lab.micrometer.note2: Standard screw + steel + bronze. One turn advances 0.5 mm, divided by 50 marks around the thimble = 0.01 mm (the same 0.5 mm screw as the interferometer [7-09]). Grades lathe parts: A = error within 10 um, B = within 20 um, C = more.
item.semiconductor-lab.micrometer.note3: In 1848 the Frenchman Jean Laurent Palmer made a tool that measures 0.01 mm with a screw. It became possible once accurate screws could be made ([8-02]).
item.semiconductor-lab.micrometer.note4: Pressing too hard squashes both part and tool slightly and shifts the reading, so micrometers have a ratchet that slips at a set force. Steel also grows about 11 um per metre per degree, so precise measurement is done at 20 C.
item.semiconductor-lab.micrometer.placeh: Approximation: real frames are cast iron or steel; here the frame is bronze.
item.semiconductor-lab.metre_bar.note1: A platinum bar that is the model of 'one metre'. Right-click two blocks to learn the length between them.
item.semiconductor-lab.metre_bar.note2: 3 platinum ingots + theodolite (returned). Right-click a block for the first mark, another block for the length in metres and old units (shaku, toise). In Minecraft one block = 1 m.
item.semiconductor-lab.metre_bar.note3: After the French Revolution, the jumble of local length units was replaced by the metre: one ten-millionth of the meridian from the North Pole to the equator. Delambre and Méchain triangulated from Dunkirk to Barcelona in 1792-98, and in 1799 a platinum bar of that length was placed in the National Archives.
item.semiconductor-lab.metre_bar.note4: The bar was an end standard: 1 m between its two end faces. Platinum was chosen because it does not rust or warp easily. In 1889 a platinum-iridium international prototype (1 m between two lines) replaced it, and in 1893 Michelson measured it in wavelengths of light (about 1.55 million waves of cadmium red). The metre was redefined by a wavelength in 1960 and by the speed of light in 1983. Japan fixed the shaku in 1891 as 10/33 of a metre.
item.semiconductor-lab.metre_bar.placeho: Approximation: the meridian survey is represented by putting the theodolite in the recipe. Lengths are measured between block centers.
item.semiconductor-lab.cast_iron_plate.n: A plate cast from pig iron in a sand mold. It is slightly warped. Rubbing three together makes them perfectly flat.

4 pig iron + sand -> 1. Hold this plate in your main hand and another plate in the other hand, then right-click: one rouge laps the two together. Two plates alone end up fitting as convex and concave. Lapping three in turn (A-B, B-C, C-A) makes all three flat, and at 1 um or less a plate becomes a surface plate.

In the 1830s-40s Whitworth spread the method of lapping three plates against each other, which makes all three flat with no outside reference. If A fits B and A fits C, then B and C have the same shape; if B also fits C, both can only be flat.

You can make something flat without anything flatter. Whitworth preferred scraping to abrasive lapping: rub with red paint, then scrape the high spots the paint marks. Flatness, squareness, screws and scales were the start of machine tools that make machines.
item.semiconductor-lab.cast_iron_plate.p: Approximation: the real method was often scraping (here plates are lapped with rouge). Casting (melting and pouring into a sand mold) is folded into the recipe.
item.semiconductor-lab.cast_iron_plate.h: Hold the plate to lap against (cast plate or surface plate) in your other hand
item.semiconductor-lab.cast_iron_plate.n: You need an abrasive (rouge) in your inventory
item.semiconductor-lab.cast_iron_plate.l: 🪨 Lapped: this plate %s um (%s), other %s um (%s) / gap between them %s um
item.semiconductor-lab.cast_iron_plate.u: Warp: not lapped yet (as cast, +-20 to 60 um)
A heavy surface plate resting on rubber. Animals walking nearby hardly shake what sits on it.

Surface plate + vulcanized rubber. Whatever sits on it shakes 1/20 as much. When you measure a mercury lamp with the interferometer, animals, minecarts or pistons moving nearby make the fringes jitter; put the lamp on an isolation table to calm them.

Precise measurement is spoiled by footsteps and traffic (around a micrometre) and by temperature. A heavy table floated on springs passes little of the fine shaking. The standard temperature for length is 20 C (chosen by the CIPM in 1931); steel grows about 11 um per metre per degree.

Today's lithography tools sit on air springs with active isolation that moves to cancel shaking, in rooms held to a hundredth of a degree. A precise factory can stop work just because a truck goes by.
Approximation: vibration sizes are game values. No air springs (compressed air) or constant temperature (20 C room, air conditioning) yet.
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.note1: A metal tube holding four lenses. Their centers are slightly off, so the image is blurred as it is.
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.note2: 4 achromatic lenses + 2 steel + 2 standard screws. Hold the barrel in your main hand and a microscope in the other, then right-click: rotate it, watch the image wobble and nudge the worst lens. When every lens is within 1 um it is centered. A simple microscope cannot see fine offsets, and a moving piston nearby hides them (stand on an isolation table).
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.note3: If a lens center (optical axis) is off, the image circles when the barrel is rotated. Skilled workers tapped the lens until the wobble vanished and locked it with a retaining ring. It was the craft of Nikon, Canon and Zeiss.
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.note4: Even the best lens blurs if assembled 0.001 mm off. Today's projection lenses align 20-30 elements to tens of nanometres, measuring the wavefront with interferometers as they are built.
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.place: Approximation: four lenses (real projection lenses have 20-30). Each tap leaving 40% is a game value. 1950 is an approximate year.
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.hold: Hold a microscope in your other hand, then right-click the lens barrel
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.wobbl: 🔬 Rotating the barrel, the image wobbles by %s um
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.canno: You cannot see any finer (limit %s um: microscope resolution %s um, floor vibration %s um)
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.tappe: Tapped lens %s into line -> offset %s um
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.done: ✨ All lens centers are within 1 um (centered)
item.semiconductor-lab.lens_barrel.unkno: Lens offsets: not inspected yet (20-80 um as assembled)
item.semiconductor-lab.centered_lens_bar: A tube whose four lens centers line up exactly. The image no longer wobbles when it turns.
A lens barrel brought within 1 um for every lens under the microscope. Material for the projection lens [7-19].
Good centering matters not only for blur but also for distortion. Copying a mask pattern onto a wafer in its true shape requires lenses on a common axis.
Even after assembly, temperature and vibration move lenses. That is why lithography tools sit on isolation tables in rooms held at 20 C ([8-07]).
item.semiconductor-lab.gauge_block_set.n: A box of steel blocks of exactly known length. Stack a few and you have a ruler of any length you like.

4 crucible steel + water bucket (quench) + rouge (finish). Right-click in the air to see how many blocks make a target length. With a micrometer in your other hand, right-click a lathe to bring its error within 1 um (a vernier caliper is too coarse).

In 1896 the Swede Johansson devised a set whose few blocks combine into tens of thousands of lengths to the micrometre. Henry Ford bought it in, and it underpinned interchangeable parts in American factories.
The faces are so flat that pressed and slid together they cling (wringing). Stacking adds almost no error, so blocks can be combined. Workshop gauges are set by comparing them with gauge blocks.
item.semiconductor-lab.gauge_block_set.p: Approximation: a 111-piece set (not the count of Johansson's first set). Finishing on a surface plate is folded into the recipe.
item.semiconductor-lab.gauge_block_set.n: Hold a micrometer in your other hand (a vernier caliper is too coarse)
item.semiconductor-lab.gauge_block_set.c: 🔧 Lathe error %s um -> %s um (set with gauge blocks and micrometer)
block.semiconductor-lab.grinder.note1: A machine that shapes hard steel precisely by wearing it away with a spinning abrasive wheel.
block.semiconductor-lab.grinder.note2: 6 steel + grinding wheel + motor + copper cable. 1 kW, 20 s. Hardened steel balls + wheel + gauge -> with a micrometer, ground balls; with gauge blocks, matched balls (the gauge and wheel are not used up).
block.semiconductor-lab.grinder.note3: Hardened steel cannot be cut with a lathe tool. In 1876 Brown & Sharpe built the universal grinding machine, and in 1883 Friedrich Fischer in Germany built a machine to grind steel balls into true spheres of one size.
block.semiconductor-lab.grinder.note4: The hard grains of the wheel take off tiny amounts in place of a cutting tool, finishing to a thousandth of a millimetre. Abrasive grains moved from natural emery to synthetic alumina and silicon carbide.
block.semiconductor-lab.grinder.placehol: Approximation: the wheel is synthetic alumina (in 1876 wheels were emery, natural corundum).
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_balls_rough: Steel rounded and quenched in water to harden it. The sizes vary a little.
Steel + water bucket -> 4. Can go straight into a bearing (small effect); grinding them on the grinder makes a better bearing.
Vaughan's 1794 carriage bearing used hand-made iron balls. With uneven balls, only the biggest ones carried the load and soon wore.
Quenching red-hot steel in water turns it into hard martensite, too hard to cut, so it is ground instead.
item.semiconductor-lab.raw_grinding_whee: A disc of hard grains held in clay. Firing it makes a grinding wheel.
2 alumina + 2 clay. Fire it in the blast furnace.
Grinding wheels are abrasive grains held by a bond such as clay and fired (vitrified wheels).
Alumina (Al2O3) is the same substance as corundum, ruby and sapphire, second only to diamond-class materials in hardness.
item.semiconductor-lab.grinding_wheel.no: A disc of hard grains fired together. It cuts by spinning.
A raw wheel fired in the blast furnace. Used to build the grinder and in its wheel slot (not used up).
As grain edges chip, fresh edges appear, so the wheel stays sharp (self-sharpening).
In 1891 Acheson made silicon carbide (carborundum), giving harder wheels. The Acheson furnace also makes graphite boats ([3-10]).
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_balls_groun: Balls ground with a wheel and sized with a micrometer.
Made on the grinder with a micrometer as the gauge. Matched to +-10 um. With 2 steel, a bearing (medium effect).
In 1883 Fischer built a machine to grind steel balls to one size, and Schweinfurt became the bearing town.
The more even the balls, the more evenly the load spreads over all of them, so the bearing lasts longer and runs smoother.
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_balls_preci: Very precise balls sized to the micrometre with gauge blocks.
Made on the grinder with gauge blocks as the gauge. Matched to +-1 um. With 2 steel, a bearing (large effect).
Mass-produced bearings sort balls into dozens of size classes and use only one class together.
Modern bearing balls can be round to within 0.1 um. Motors, hard disks and lithography stages all ride on precise balls.
item.semiconductor-lab.ball_bearing.note: A part with steel balls between shaft and housing. They roll instead of rubbing, so it turns easily.

2 steel + steel balls. Right-click a rotating machine (lathe, compressor, wafer saw, polisher, resist coater, CZ puller) to install it and lower its power use (grade 1 5%, grade 2 15%, grade 3 30%). Furnaces and tanks take none. It drops when the machine is broken.
1794 Vaughan (carriages), 1869 bicycles, 1883 mass production with Fischer's ground balls, 1907 SKF's self-aligning bearing. Almost everything that turns has ball bearings.
Plain bearings have friction coefficients of about 0.01-0.1, ball bearings about 0.001-0.005. ⚠️ How much a whole machine's power drops is a game value (5-30%).
item.semiconductor-lab.ball_bearing.plac: Approximation: the power reductions (x0.95, x0.85, x0.70) are game values.
item.semiconductor-lab.ball_bearing.not_: This machine has no rotating shaft (no bearing fits)
item.semiconductor-lab.ball_screw.note1: A screw with small steel balls rolling between the thread and the nut. Nothing slides, so it moves very finely and lightly.
item.semiconductor-lab.ball_screw.note2: Lead screw + steel + steel balls (grade 1-3 from the balls). In a lathe's master-screw slot it shrinks the error of the screws it makes (grade 1 half, grade 2 a quarter, grade 3 a tenth) and saves a little power. Feed resolution 5/2/1 um (a lead screw: 10 um).
item.semiconductor-lab.ball_screw.note3: In 1898 Stevenson and Glenn in the USA patented the ball screw. It spread through recirculating-ball car steering (around 1939), and in 1952 it met MIT's numerically controlled milling machine, starting micrometre positioning.
item.semiconductor-lab.ball_screw.note4: An ordinary screw sticks and then suddenly slips when it starts to move (stick-slip), so it cannot make tiny moves. Rolling balls avoid this, giving the fine feed of a lithography stage.
item.semiconductor-lab.ball_screw.placeh: Approximation: feed resolution and the error and power reductions are game values.
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_saw.note1: A saw with diamond on its blade, for cutting hard things.
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_saw.note2: Diamond + 2 iron + stick. With rock crystal it makes a quartz blank (the saw returns).
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_saw.note3: Quartz is very hard (Mohs 7), so ordinary blades cannot cut it. The blade carries grains of diamond, the hardest material.
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_saw.note4: Silicon wafers and chips are also cut (dicing [9-32]) with thin disc blades carrying diamond grains.
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_blank.note: A thin plate cut from quartz in a set direction. Its thickness decides how fast it vibrates.
Rock crystal + diamond saw. Hold it and right-click to lap it 20 um thinner with one rouge (the frequency rises). With a silver nugget it becomes a crystal resonator.
In 1921 Cady in the USA built an oscillator whose frequency was set by a quartz plate. The AT cut (1934) barely changes frequency with temperature.
Frequency is inversely proportional to thickness (AT cut: f = 1661 kHz mm / thickness). Factories trim the frequency exactly by lapping or adding metal little by little.
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_blank.too_: Any thinner and it will crack
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_blank.beat: ⏱ This crystal vibrates %s times a second
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_blank.moni: 📏 Thickness monitor: %s evaporations, %s nm silver -> frequency down %s Hz
item.semiconductor-lab.crystal_resonator: A quartz blank with electrodes. It vibrates at a very precise rate, so it is the heart of clocks and computers.

Quartz blank + silver nugget (electrodes). Right-click in the air to hear how many times a second it vibrates. Right-click a vacuum evaporator for a thickness monitor (the film's mass lowers the frequency).
In 1927 Marrison at Bell Labs built the quartz clock. In a wristwatch a tuning-fork quartz vibrates 32,768 times a second (2 multiplied 15 times).
In 1959 Sauerbrey showed that a film on quartz lowers its frequency (df = 2.26e-6 f0^2 dm/A). Evaporator thickness monitors measure nanometre films this way.
Approximation: each evaporation adds 50 nm of silver. Depositing the electrodes and wiring to an oscillator circuit are skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrothermal_char: Quartz scraps, alkali and a seed crystal packed together, to grow quartz in hot water.

4 vein quartz + sodium hydroxide + rock crystal (seed). In the autoclave with water at 280 C and 15 atm or more for 40 s -> 3 cultured quartz. Without enough pressure it comes back unchanged. ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion (sodium hydroxide).
World War II left radios short of (Brazilian) quartz, so from the late 1940s Bell Labs and others developed ways to grow quartz in factories.

Quartz scraps and alkaline water sit at the bottom of a steel pressure vessel with seed crystals hung above. Heating the bottom dissolves the quartz, which crystallizes on the seeds in the slightly cooler top (hydrothermal growth), just as quartz forms in hot water underground.
Approximation: really about 350 C and over 1000 atm for weeks (the game autoclave tops out at 300 C and 20 atm). The top-bottom temperature difference is skipped.
item.semiconductor-lab.cultured_quartz.n: Quartz grown in a factory vessel. Fewer flaws than natural crystal and a regular shape.
3 from a hydrothermal charge in the autoclave. A diamond saw cuts it into quartz blanks (for crystal resonators).
Almost all quartz in today's resonators is cultured. Japan became a major producer.
Seeds are oriented, so the crystals are easy to cut in set directions. This differs from optical synthetic silica glass [7-15], which is glass made by burning SiCl4.
block.semiconductor-lab.ruling_engine.no: A machine that rules tens of thousands of fine grooves on a mirror with a diamond, advancing a very precise screw a little each time.

2 lead screws + surface plate + motor + 5 iron. 300 W, 60 s. Mirror (speculum or silvered) + diamond (not used up) + lead screw (not used up) -> ruled grating (600 lines/mm). If the floor shakes or the temperature changes without air conditioning at the end of ruling, the grating shows false lines (ghosts).

In 1882 Rowland at Johns Hopkins built a ruling engine with a screw he perfected himself, ruling hundreds of grooves per millimetre and sending concave gratings around the world. A grating took days, and a small temperature change could ruin it.

Small periodic errors of the screw shift the groove spacing and produce false lines called ghosts beside the real ones, so ruling engines lived in basement rooms of constant temperature. Ramsden's 1775 dividing engine (ruling precise circle scales) is an ancestor of the same technique.
block.semiconductor-lab.ruling_engine.pl: Approximation: time (60 s), power and the ghost conditions (50 nm vibration, 1 C) are game values.
item.semiconductor-lab.ruled_grating.not: A plate with many fine grooves ruled into a mirror. It splits light finely, like a rainbow.
Made on the ruling engine (600 lines/mm, 30000 over 50 mm). With a spectroscope it makes a ruled-grating spectroscope.
Finer spacing bends light more, and more grooves separate closer colors (wavelengths): resolving power R = number of grooves.
Modern gratings are made by recording interference fringes in resist (holographic gratings). Lithography stage encoders also use fine gratings to measure position.
item.semiconductor-lab.ruled_spectroscop: A spectroscope that splits light with a fine grating and shows it very sharply.
Ruled grating + spectroscope. Used like the spectroscope. Sodium's yellow D line shows as two lines, 589.0 and 589.6 nm (one line with the wire grating). A grating with ghosts also shows false lines.
With Rowland's gratings the wavelengths of thousands of dark lines in sunlight were measured precisely and compared with elements on Earth (Rowland's solar spectrum tables, 1890s).
Splitting a doublet needs resolving power lambda / delta-lambda (about 982 for the D lines). A grating's resolving power is grooves x order.
block.semiconductor-lab.electron_microsc: A microscope that looks with electrons instead of light, showing things far too fine for light.

4 steel + tungsten wire + 2 copper cable + transformer + rectifier. 2 kW. Works only with an adjacent vacuum chamber at 0.01 Pa or less (diffusion pump). Put a mask or wafer in the slot to compare with the optical microscope and see whether its fine lines are visible.
In 1931 Ruska and Knoll in Germany focused electrons with copper-coil magnetic lenses, and in 1933 surpassed the optical microscope's resolution. Ruska received the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Electrons are waves too (de Broglie 1924); accelerated by tens of kV their wavelength is about 1/100,000 of light. Lens aberrations limited real resolution to about 10 nm by the late 1930s. Fabs today measure circuit line widths with scanning electron microscopes (SEM, 1965).
Approximation: 10 nm resolution is a late-1930s guide. No scanning mode or thin sectioning.
gui.semiconductor-lab.electron_microscop: Pump the next chamber below 0.01 Pa
Coarse enough for the optical one too
item.semiconductor-lab.mass_spectrometer: Sorts atoms by weight. Shows that one element can have members of different weight (isotopes).

Crafting: 2 electromagnets + 4 soda-lime glass + 1 mercury diffusion pump + 2 iron + 1 copper cable → 1. Hold a sample in the other hand (B2O3, phosphorus, chlorine, argon, hydrogen, silicon, germanium, copper, lead, gold) and right-click to list its isotopes and their shares.

The sample is ionised and sent through an electromagnet, where the ions curve in circles. Lighter ions curve more, so where they land tells their mass. The inside is kept at high vacuum so they do not hit air.

In 1913 J. J. Thomson found two kinds of neon of different weight, and in 1919 Aston built a mass spectrograph and found isotopes of many elements (1922 Nobel Prize in Chemistry). An ion implanter uses the same idea to pick only ¹¹B for boron before it hits the wafer.
Approximation: hold it and right-click for the result (a real one needs an ion source, high voltage and a photographic plate or detector). Shares are natural abundances.
Only one isotope (all atoms weigh the same)
Hold a sample in the other hand
This sample cannot be analysed yet
item.semiconductor-lab.kilogram_prototyp: The model of one kilogram. Until 2019 the world's kilogram was the mass of one lump of metal like this.
Platinum ingot + rouge (polishing). Right-click with another prototype in the other hand to see the difference on a balance (ug). As days pass, surface contamination makes the gap grow.

In 1799 a platinum kilogram was deposited in the Paris Archives with the metre bar. In 1889 a 90% platinum, 10% iridium cylinder (about 39 mm high and wide) became the International Prototype, and copies went to each country (Japan has No. 6).

Over about 100 years the prototype and its copies drifted about 50 ug apart (50 parts per billion). Whether the prototype got lighter or the copies heavier, nobody could tell by definition. This led to the 2019 redefinition using the Kibble balance and Planck's constant.
Approximation: the real International Prototype is 90% Pt, 10% Ir (iridium cannot be made yet, so pure platinum = the 1799 kilogram). The drift rate is sped up for the game.
⚖ On the balance this one is %s ug (%s parts per billion). Ages %s and %s days
Nearly equal: within the finishing tolerance
They have drifted apart. Which is the true 1 kg? By definition nobody can check the prototype itself
⚖ The prototype is exactly 1 kg by definition (made %s days ago). Hold another prototype in the other hand to compare
item.semiconductor-lab.krypton_lamp.note: A lamp that makes krypton gas glow. The waves of its orange light once defined the length of one metre.

Quartz tube + krypton bag + 2 tungsten wires. Hold it in the hand opposite the interferometer and right-click two blocks in turn: the distance is counted in krypton wavelengths (no metre bar needed). Right-click in the air for the SI. Lasts 64 uses.

In 1960 the 11th General Conference on Weights and Measures created the International System of Units (SI) and redefined the metre as 1,650,763.73 wavelengths of krypton-86's orange line. The metre bar retired. SI base units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, candela (the mole joined in 1971, making 7). Prefixes include kilo (thousand), milli (thousandth) and micro (millionth).

An atom's wavelength is the same wherever and by whoever it is made, so it is a surer ruler than a metal bar. In 1983 the metre became the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 s. In 2019 the kilogram was tied to Planck's constant, so all seven units now rest on constants of nature.
item.semiconductor-lab.krypton_lamp.plac: Approximation: the real lamp used isolated krypton-86 (about 17% of natural krypton) cooled to the triple point of nitrogen (about -210 C). Here it is natural krypton.
item.semiconductor-lab.weston_cell.note1: A cell made not to deliver power but to always give the same voltage (1.0186 V): a ruler for voltage.
item.semiconductor-lab.weston_cell.note2: Soda-lime glass (H-shaped tube) + mercury + cadmium + sulfuric acid + 2 platinum grains (leads). Voltage reference for the Kibble balance. It passes almost no current, so it does not wear. It drifts about 40 uV per degree, so an air conditioner makes it more accurate. ⚠ Contains mercury and cadmium.
item.semiconductor-lab.weston_cell.note3: Made by Edward Weston in 1893. From 1911 to 1990 the world's volt was kept with these cells.
item.semiconductor-lab.weston_cell.note4: One side is cadmium amalgam, the other mercury with mercury(I) sulfate, joined by saturated cadmium sulfate solution. Since 1990 the volt comes from the superconducting Josephson effect (cooled with liquid helium) ⚠️ (explained only, as this mod does not use helium).
item.semiconductor-lab.weston_cell.place: Approximation: making cadmium sulfate and mercury(I) sulfate is skipped; the cell is made from the raw materials.
item.semiconductor-lab.standard_resistor: A coil of metal wire whose resistance barely changes with temperature: a ruler for resistance.
Copper + nickel (constantan wire) + iron (case). Resistance reference for the Kibble balance.

In the 1880s alloys whose resistance barely changes with temperature were found, such as copper-nickel constantan and copper-manganese-nickel manganin (1889), and standard resistors sealed in oil were made.
Since 1990 resistance has been fixed by the quantum Hall effect, seen in strong magnetic fields at very low temperatures ⚠️ (explained only).
Approximation: real standard resistors use manganin (manganese is not available yet, so constantan).
block.semiconductor-lab.kibble_balance.n: A balance that weighs a mass against an electric force. Today's kilogram is set with balances like this.

2 magnets + copper (coil) + interferometer + 5 steel. 200 W, 30 s. With a kilogram prototype, Weston cell, standard resistor and krypton-86 lamp it gives the prototype's offset from 1 kg and its uncertainty. An air conditioner nearby (+-0.1 C swing) and a vacuum chamber next to it (no air buoyancy) shrink the uncertainty.

Proposed in 1975 by Bryan Kibble at the UK National Physical Laboratory. In weighing mode the coil force balances the weight; in moving mode the coil moves and a voltage is measured; the magnet's strength cancels, leaving mgv = UI. It was renamed after Kibble, who died in 2016.

Measuring voltage with the Josephson effect and resistance with the quantum Hall effect ties mass to Planck's constant h. In 2019 the kilogram was redefined by fixing h = 6.62607015e-34 J s. This mod's classical version (standard cell and resistor) reaches about 1e-6 (a few mg), so the 50 ug drift between prototypes stays hidden ⚠️.
block.semiconductor-lab.kibble_balance.p: Approximation: classical standard cell and resistor instead of quantum standards (Josephson, quantum Hall, liquid helium). Measuring g and the magnet and coil details are skipped. Uncertainty figures are typical game values.
item.semiconductor-lab.sextant.note1: A tool that uses two mirrors to bring the sun down to the horizon and measure its height. The midday sun's height tells you where on Earth (latitude) you are.
item.semiconductor-lab.sextant.note2: Silvered mirror + refracting telescope + half-silvered mirror + vernier caliper + 3 bronze. Right-click several times before noon where you can see the sky. When the sun peaks and starts to fall, latitude = 90 deg - highest angle. With a chronometer in the other hand you also get longitude. In this world z = 0 is the equator and 1000 blocks north is 1 deg of latitude.
item.semiconductor-lab.sextant.note3: In 1731 John Hadley in England presented the reflecting octant, and Thomas Godfrey in America made one at about the same time. Around 1757 the scale was widened into the sextant so the moon-to-star angle could be measured too. Sailing navigators measured the sun every noon (the noon sight).
item.semiconductor-lab.sextant.note4: Turning the moving mirror by theta turns the reflected light by 2 theta, so a 60 deg arc (one sixth of a circle) measures up to 120 deg. Latitude also comes from the height of the Pole Star. Cutting accurate scales needed a dividing engine (Ramsden, 1775).
item.semiconductor-lab.sextant.placehold: Approximation: no seasons (the sun always stands over the equator). The scale of latitude and longitude (1 deg = 1000 blocks; real about 111 km) and the sky's sun moving at the same time everywhere are game conveniences.
item.semiconductor-lab.sextant.again: Measure again a little later to see whether it is rising or falling
item.semiconductor-lab.sextant.rising: Still rising. Keep measuring until it culminates (highest)
item.semiconductor-lab.sextant.falling: Falling: noon has passed. Measure again tomorrow before noon
item.semiconductor-lab.sextant.noon: 🧭 Noon! Highest angle %s -> latitude = 90 deg - noon altitude = %s %s
item.semiconductor-lab.sextant.longitude: 🕰 Greenwich time then %s -> longitude = (12:00 - time) x 15 deg = %s %s
item.semiconductor-lab.sextant.need_cloc: For longitude too, hold a clock that carries Greenwich time (a chronometer) in the other hand
item.semiconductor-lab.sextant.no_sky: Cannot see the sky and horizon (not under a roof, in rain, or outside the Overworld)
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_watch.note: A wristwatch whose IC counts a tiny quartz plate vibrating 32,768 times a second to make one second.

Crystal resonator + IC (plastic package) + stepping motor + dry cell + crown glass + iron. Right-click for Greenwich time. It drifts about +-0.2 s a day (a spring-driven wristwatch about +-10 s). With another clock in the other hand you see their difference; with a sextant it also measures longitude.
In 1927 Bell Labs built a quartz clock the size of a room. In December 1969 Suwa Seikosha (Seiko) in Japan released the world's first quartz wristwatch, the Quartz Astron 35SQ.
32,768 is 2 to the 15th, so 15 divide-by-two stages in the IC give exactly one second. The quartz is cut as a tuning fork whose frequency barely changes with temperature.
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_watch.plac: Approximation: it takes the same crystal plate as the film-thickness monitor (real watch crystals are 32,768 Hz tuning forks). Any IC chip will do.
item.semiconductor-lab.droplet_generator: A device that pushes molten tin through a fine nozzle and breaks it into even little drops. A relative of the inkjet printer.
4 steel + crystal resonator (piezo vibration) + quartz tube (nozzle) + tungsten wire (heater). Part of the EUV light source. Right-click for droplet size, spacing and rate.

In 1880 the Curie brothers found that squeezing quartz makes a voltage (piezoelectricity), and the next year confirmed that a voltage makes it stretch. In 1878 Rayleigh explained why a liquid jet breaks into evenly spaced drops. From around 2006, EUV sources fired CO2 lasers at tin droplets.

Surface tension pinches a liquid jet every ~4.5 jet diameters into drops ~1.9 diameters across. Vibrating the nozzle with quartz evens the spacing, and several drops are merged into about 50,000 drops a second, about 30 um across.
Approximation: 16 um nozzle and 70 m/s are typical values. Droplet merging is not modelled.
💧 Nozzle %s um -> droplets about %s um, pinched every %s um -> about %s drops a second (real sources merge them to about 50,000)
item.semiconductor-lab.simple_pulley.not: A wheel with a rope over it. It changes the direction of the pull but does not make the load lighter.
Planks + stick + rope. Right-click a block to see the force needed to lift one (1 m3). Four make a compound pulley.
Pull down and the load goes up, like a well bucket. Used since ancient times.
One rope carries the whole weight, so the force equals the weight (m x 9.8 N).
item.semiconductor-lab.compound_pulley.n: A set of wheels that lets a small force lift a heavy load.
4 simple pulleys + 2 rope (four ropes carry the load). The force to lift a right-clicked block is a quarter, but you pull four times the rope. Shows whether a person (about 400 N) can lift it.
Vitruvius in ancient Rome and Hero of Alexandria described compound-pulley cranes ⚠️.
Force x rope pulled = weight x height raised (the work is the same). Four ropes share the weight, so each carries a quarter.
item.semiconductor-lab.compound_pulley.p: Approximation: block masses use typical densities and a person pulls 400 N. Friction is ignored.
